spec.title: Read the control on the wire
spec.intro:
You are handed real captured network traffic and asked to read three control claims directly
off the bytes — "only 443 is exposed," "encrypted in transit," "the L2 trust assumption holds" —
then diagnose the single byte where a real broken capture contradicts its claim.

This surface is the packet itself, rendered as nested byte-range regions. A layer stays closed
until you read the selector byte that justifies opening the next one. Every value you reveal is
the dissector's real decode of the real bytes — the same value tshark produces. Nothing is
invented; the packet is the answer key. Start on the clean capture (Pair A · clean).

tasks.instruction:
On the clean capture, select the `EtherType` region (Ethernet bytes 12–13), label it with
its OSI layer, and read the value that tells the dissector the payload is IPv4.

hints.nudge: The frame begins with two MAC addresses (6 bytes each); the 2-byte type tag follows.

hints.concept: §4.1 — the selector byte opens the next box; EtherType names the L3 payload

hints.reveal: Select bytes 12–13 (EtherType), label it L2; it reads 0x0800 = IPv4

tasks.explain:
You just read the first selector. `0x0800` is the byte that *chose* the IPv4 parser — the
same choice the network made. Ethernet is L2; reading its EtherType earned you the right to
open the box inside.

tasks.instruction:
Descend into IPv4 (now unlocked). Select the `Protocol` field (IPv4 offset 9), label the
IPv4 region's layer, and read which L4 parser this byte selects.

hints.nudge: RFC 791 fixes the IPv4 header; the L4 selector is one byte, nine in.

hints.reveal: Select the Protocol byte (IPv4 offset 9), label it L3; it reads 0x06 = 6 = TCP

tasks.explain:
The second selector. `0x06` chose the TCP parser. IPv4 is L3 — the end-to-end layer. Notice
the TCP region stayed gated until you read this byte: you cannot peel a layer you have not
earned the selector for.

tasks.instruction:
Select the IPv4 `Destination Address` region (L3) and read the end-to-end address. This —
not the MAC — is what attributes the host across a routed boundary.

hints.nudge: The IPv4 destination address sits at IP offset 16–19 (four bytes).

hints.concept: §4.2 — MAC is hop-truth (rewritten each hop); IP is end-to-end-truth (preserved)

hints.reveal: Select the Destination Address region (L3); it reads 142.251.152.119

tasks.explain:
A router rewrites the MAC at every hop, so a logged MAC names only the last forwarder. The IP
is preserved end-to-end — it is the address that attributes the originating host. Scope is
which bytes change when the packet moves.

tasks.instruction:
Descend into TCP. Select the `Destination Port` region and read it. This field decides the
"only 443 is exposed" claim (CM-7 / SC-7).

hints.nudge: The TCP header opens with source then destination port (two bytes each).

hints.concept: §4.3 — the 5-tuple is the firewall's whole worldview; dst-port is exposure

hints.reveal: Select the Destination Port region (L4); it reads 443

tasks.explain:
Destination port 443 satisfies "only 443 is exposed." A packet to 80 here would be the
finding. This is one of the five fields a firewall rule decides on — you can now read any
ACL as a predicate over them.

tasks.instruction:
Descend to the TLS record and select the `ContentType` byte (the record's first byte). Label
its layer. This — not the port — is where "encrypted in transit" actually lives.

hints.nudge: RFC 8446 puts the ContentType as the very first byte of every TLS record.

hints.reveal: Select the ContentType byte (TLS record byte 0), label it L6; 0x16 = 22 = handshake

tasks.explain:
The port was a promise; the ContentType is the proof, and it lives at a different layer (L6).
`0x16` is the still-cleartext handshake; `0x17` would be opaque application data. Reaching for
the port to prove encryption is the classic mistake — the ContentType is the fix.

tasks.instruction:
Select the TCP `Flags` region (offset 13) and read its decoded value. The connection's state
is literally readable in this one byte — contrast it with the handshake's SYN/SYN+ACK/ACK.

hints.nudge: The eight TCP control flags share one byte at TCP offset 13.

hints.concept: §4.4 — the flags ARE the state: SYN opens, SYN+ACK accepts, ACK confirms

hints.reveal: Select the Flags region (L4); this established-connection segment reads PSH+ACK

tasks.explain:
The flag bits carry the connection's state in one byte. The three-way handshake reads
0x02 (SYN) → 0x12 (SYN+ACK) → 0x10 (ACK); this mid-stream segment has ACK set. Read the byte,
read the state — and a real TCP counterpart answers a wrong order with a RST, not "try again."

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the broken Pair-A capture (the tab labelled "pair-a-port-exposure · broken"). Select
the single field where this real capture contradicts the "only 443 is exposed" claim.

hints.nudge: Both captures are real and nearly identical — exactly one field carries the violation.

hints.concept: §4.7 — a control is a predicate over bytes; exposure lives at the L4 dst-port

hints.reveal: On the broken tab, select the Destination Port (L4) — it reads 80, not 443

tasks.explain:
The discriminating byte is the dissector's computed divergence over two real captures, not
your opinion: destination port 80 where the claim says 443 breaks CM-7 / SC-7. Your Wire
Evidence Finding names the field, both values, the control, and the framework reference — and
anyone can re-derive it from the same bytes.

tasks.instruction:
In 4–6 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain encapsulation as nested boxes and how
one selector byte opens the next; why "encrypted in transit" lives at the TLS ContentType and
not the port; and why the IP — not the MAC — attributes a host across a routed hop. Use the
§3 mailing-the-letter model, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 model: a crate inside a box inside a letter — each layer reads only its own label.
